at gifte sig.explanation: "At gifte sig" means "to get married". The little word "sig" changes to match who is marrying: "du gifter dig" (you get married), "han gifter sig" (he gets married). "Gift" on its own means "married": "Jeg er gift" (I am married).

sentence.da: De vil **gifte sig** i kirken, og hun har en hvid kjole.
sentence.en: They want to get married in the church, and she has a white dress.

at give.explanation: "At give" means "to give": "Jeg giver dig bogen" (I give you the book). It is part of many phrases, such as "at give op" (to give up) and "at give besked" (to let someone know).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **give** dig min bog, så du kan læse den.
sentence.en: I will give you my book so you can read it.

at glemme.explanation: "At glemme" means "to forget", both facts and things you were meant to bring or do: "Jeg glemte at ringe" (I forgot to call).

sentence.da: Jeg må ikke **glemme** min paraply, for det regner.
sentence.en: I must not forget my umbrella, because it is raining.

at godtage.explanation: "At godtage" means "to accept" something, like an explanation, an offer or a rule, and it sounds fairly formal. In everyday speech "at acceptere" (to accept) is just as common. "At tage imod" (to receive) is for taking something you are given.

sentence.da: Prisen er for høj, så vi kan ikke **godtage** tilbuddet.
sentence.en: The price is too high, so we cannot accept the offer.

at grine.explanation: "At grine" means "to laugh", usually out loud at something funny: "Vi grinede meget" (We laughed a lot). Be careful with "grine af" (to laugh at someone), which can sound unkind.

sentence.da: Klovnen er så sjov, at børnene vil **grine**.
sentence.en: The clown is so funny that the children will laugh.

at græde.explanation: "At græde" means "to cry", usually when people are sad. "Hvorfor græder du?" means "Why are you crying?".

sentence.da: Hvis du er meget ked af det, kan du **græde**.
sentence.en: If you are very sad, you can cry.

at gå.explanation: "At gå" means "to go on foot", so "to walk", and also "to leave": "Jeg går nu" (I am leaving now). It also describes how things are going ("Det går godt" means "It is going well") and is used for buses and trains that run. For going by car or plane, use "at køre" (to drive) or "at flyve" (to fly) instead.

sentence.da: Jeg kan **gå** til skole, for den ligger tæt på.
sentence.en: I can walk to school, because it is close by.

forms.en: I have been for a walk

at gå en tur.explanation: "At gå en tur" means "to go for a walk", just for pleasure or fresh air. You can add where: "gå en tur i parken" (go for a walk in the park). "En tur" can also mean "a trip", as in "en tur til Aarhus" (a trip to Aarhus), so the situation tells you which is meant.

sentence.da: Vi vil **gå en tur** i parken, fordi solen skinner.
sentence.en: We want to go for a walk in the park, because the sun is shining.

at gå hjem.explanation: "At gå hjem" means "to walk home", or more loosely "to head home". It is about going on foot. By car, say "at køre hjem" (to drive home). "At tage hjem" (to go home) works whatever way you travel.

sentence.da: Det er sent, så vi skal **gå hjem** og sove.
sentence.en: It is late, so we have to go home and sleep.

forms.en: I have gone to the movies

at gå i biografen.explanation: "At gå i biografen" means "to go to the cinema". Literally it is "to walk in the cinema", but it is the normal phrase even if you drive. Some Danes also say the shorter "at gå i bio" (to go to the cinema).

sentence.da: Vi vil **gå i biografen** og se en film.
sentence.en: We want to go to the movies and see a film.

at gå i seng.explanation: "At gå i seng" means "to go to bed". Danish leaves out "en" (a) before "seng" (bed). Falling asleep is something different: "at falde i søvn" (to fall asleep).

sentence.da: Børnene skal **gå i seng**, for det er sent, og de er trætte.
sentence.en: The children have to go to bed, because it is late and they are tired.

at gå ind.explanation: "At gå ind" means "to go in", walking into a place such as a room or a house. Danish has two little words: "ind" for going in, and "inde" for being inside: "Han er inde i huset" (He is inside the house).

sentence.da: Det regner, så vi skal **gå ind** i huset.
sentence.en: It is raining, so we have to go into the house.

at gå ned.explanation: "At gå ned" means "to go down", such as walking down the stairs. It is also used for the sun: "solen går ned" means "the sun sets".

sentence.da: Elevatoren er i stykker, så vi skal **gå ned** ad trappen.
sentence.en: The lift is broken, so we have to walk down the stairs.

at gå op.explanation: "At gå op" means "to go up", such as walking up the stairs or to an upper floor. It is also used for the sun: "solen går op" means "the sun rises".

sentence.da: Elevatoren er i stykker, så vi skal **gå op** ad trappen til tredje sal.
sentence.en: The lift is broken, so we have to walk up the stairs to the third floor.

forms.en: I have gone to a café

at gå på café.explanation: "At gå på café" means "to go to a café". Danish says "på café" (literally "on café") with no "en" (a), and the same goes for "på restaurant" (to a restaurant).

sentence.da: Vi vil **gå på café** og drikke en kop kaffe.
sentence.en: We want to go to a café and drink a cup of coffee.

at gå tilbage.explanation: "At gå tilbage" means "to go back", returning to where you came from: "Jeg går tilbage til hotellet" (I walk back to the hotel). It is about going on foot. By car, say "at køre tilbage" (to drive back).

sentence.da: Jeg har glemt min taske, så jeg skal **gå tilbage** til caféen.
sentence.en: I have forgotten my bag, so I have to go back to the café.

at gå ud.explanation: "At gå ud" means "to go out", either to leave a place such as the house, or to go out for the evening, for example to a bar or restaurant: "Skal vi gå ud?" (Shall we go out?).

sentence.da: Solen skinner, så vi vil **gå ud** i haven.
sentence.en: The sun is shining, so we want to go out into the garden.

at gå væk.explanation: "At gå væk" means "to go away" or "to walk off", leaving a place. As a command, "Gå væk!" means "Go away!", which sounds rude, so be careful.

sentence.da: Hunden bjæffer, så katten vil **gå væk**.
sentence.en: The dog is barking, so the cat wants to go away.

at gøre.explanation: "At gøre" means "to do", as in "Hvad gør du?" (What are you doing?). It can stand in for an action you do not want to repeat: "Jeg læser, og det gør hun også" (I am reading, and she does too). For making things, such as food, Danish uses "at lave" (to make): "at lave mad" (to cook).

sentence.da: Jeg ved ikke, hvad jeg skal **gøre**, når bussen ikke kommer.
sentence.en: I do not know what to do when the bus does not come.

at gøre ondt.explanation: "At gøre ondt" means "to hurt", the standard way to say something is painful. The part that hurts comes first: "Min fod gør ondt" (My foot hurts). You can also say "Jeg har ondt i foden" (I have a pain in the foot), which literally says "the foot" where English says "my foot".

sentence.da: Hvis du falder, vil det **gøre ondt**.
sentence.en: If you fall, it will hurt.

at gøre rent.explanation: "At gøre rent" means "to clean" a place, for example the house or the kitchen. It is built from "gøre" (to do) and "rent" (clean), so literally "to make clean". "At rengøre" (to clean) also exists.

sentence.da: Vi skal **gøre rent**, så huset ikke er beskidt.
sentence.en: We have to clean, so the house is not dirty.

en gade.explanation: "En gade" means "a street", a road in a town with houses on both sides. Street names often end in "-gade", like "Nørregade" (North Street). For a bigger road, for example between towns, use "en vej" (a road).

sentence.da: Vi går ned ad en lang **gade** med mange huse og butikker.
sentence.en: We walk down a long street with many houses and shops.

en gaffel.explanation: "En gaffel" means "a fork". You eat "med en gaffel" (with a fork), and "kniv og gaffel" means "knife and fork".

sentence.da: Jeg skærer kødet med en kniv og spiser det med en **gaffel**.
sentence.en: I cut the meat with a knife and eat it with a fork.

en gang om ugen.explanation: "En gang om ugen" means "once a week". Change the number to say how often: "to gange om ugen" (twice a week), "tre gange om ugen" (three times a week). Change the last word to change the time: "en gang om dagen" (once a day), "en gang om måneden" (once a month).

sentence.da: Jeg træner **en gang om ugen**, hver mandag.
sentence.en: I work out once a week, every Monday.

en giraf.explanation: "En giraf" means "a giraffe". Watch the spelling: "giraf" has one "f", but "giraffen" and "giraffer" have two.

sentence.da: En **giraf** har en meget lang hals og spiser blade fra træerne.
sentence.en: A giraffe has a very long neck and eats leaves from the trees.

en gris.explanation: "En gris" means "a pig". Pork is "svinekød", built from "et svin" (a swine), another word for pig. Calling a person "en gris" is rude, as with "pig" in English. A baby pig is "en pattegris" (a piglet).

sentence.da: En **gris** er lyserød, og den ligger gerne i mudderet.
sentence.en: A pig is pink, and it likes to lie in the mud.

en grund.explanation: "En grund" means "a reason". "Af den grund" means "for that reason". It can also mean a plot of land that you build on.

sentence.da: Der er ingen **grund** til at være bange.
sentence.en: There is no reason to be afraid.

en grøntsag.explanation: "En grøntsag" means "a vegetable". It is built from "grøn" (green) and "sag" (thing), so it is literally a "green thing". Ask "Spiser du grøntsager?" for "Do you eat vegetables?".

sentence.da: En gulerod er en **grøntsag**, og et æble er en frugt.
sentence.en: A carrot is a vegetable, and an apple is a fruit.

en guitar.explanation: "En guitar" means "a guitar". Danish has no word for "the" when you play it: "Jeg spiller guitar" is "I play guitar", using "at spille" (to play).

sentence.da: Min bror spiller **guitar** og synger i et band.
sentence.en: My brother plays guitar and sings in a band.

en gulerod.explanation: "En gulerod" means "a carrot". It is built from "gul" (yellow) and "rod" (root), so it is literally a "yellow root".

sentence.da: Kaninen spiser en orange **gulerod**.
sentence.en: The rabbit eats an orange carrot.

en gåtur.explanation: "En gåtur" means "a walk", usually for pleasure or fresh air. It is built from "gå" (walk) and "tur" (trip). You say "at gå en tur" or "at tage på gåtur", both meaning "to go for a walk".

sentence.da: Vi tager på **gåtur** i skoven og går i to timer.
sentence.en: We go for a walk in the forest and walk for two hours.

en gæst.explanation: "En gæst" means "a guest", for visitors in your home and also for hotel guests. "Vi får gæster" means "We are having guests".

sentence.da: Vi har en **gæst** i aften, så jeg laver ekstra mad.
sentence.en: We have a guest tonight, so I am making extra food.

et gavekort.explanation: "Et gavekort" means "a gift card", a card with money on it that you give as a present. It is made of "en gave" (a gift) and "et kort" (a card).

sentence.da: Jeg ved ikke, hvad han vil have, så jeg giver ham et **gavekort**.
sentence.en: I do not know what he wants, so I give him a gift card.

et glas.explanation: "Et glas" means "a glass", both the material and a drinking glass. Danish has no word for "of" here: "et glas vand" is "a glass of water" and "et glas vin" is "a glass of wine".

sentence.da: Kan jeg få et **glas** vand?
sentence.en: Can I have a glass of water?

et gram.explanation: "Et gram" means "a gram", a unit of weight. "Hundrede gram" means "a hundred grams".

sentence.da: Jeg skal bruge to hundrede **gram** mel.
sentence.en: I need two hundred grams of flour.

et gulv.explanation: "Et gulv" means "a floor", the surface you walk on in a room. For a level of a building, such as "the second floor", Danes say "en etage" (a level of a building).

sentence.da: Vi har malet væggene og lagt et nyt **gulv**.
sentence.en: We have painted the walls and laid a new floor.

gammel.explanation: "Gammel" means "old", for things ("en gammel bil", an old car) and for a person's age. To ask age you say "Hvor gammel er du?" (How old are you?) and answer "Jeg er tredive år gammel" (I am thirty years old).

sentence.da: Min bedstefar er 90 år og meget **gammel**.
sentence.en: My grandfather is 90 years old and very old.

gang.explanation: "Gang" means "a time" in the sense of an occasion: "en gang" means "once" and "to gange" means "twice". It can also mean a hallway in a house. Do not mix it up with "tid" (time in general). "Hvor mange gange?" means "How many times?".

sentence.da: Jeg har været i Paris en **gang**, men ikke to gange.
sentence.en: I have been to Paris once, but not twice.

forms.en: I am happy to do that.

gerne.explanation: "Gerne" means "gladly" and makes you sound polite. Compare "Jeg vil have kaffe" (I want coffee), which sounds blunt, with "Jeg vil gerne have kaffe" (I would like coffee). On its own it is a friendly yes: "Ska' vi gå?" - "Ja, gerne!" (Shall we go? - Yes, gladly!). "Det gør jeg gerne" means "I am happy to do that".

sentence.da: Jeg vil **gerne** have en kop te.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of tea.

gift.explanation: "Gift" means "married". "Jeg er gift" means "I am married", and you add "med" (with) for the partner: "gift med Peter" (married to Peter). Careful: "gift" is also the word for poison, so context shows which one is meant.

sentence.da: Jeg er **gift** med Anna. Hun er min kone.
sentence.en: I am married to Anna. She is my wife.

glad.explanation: "Glad" means "happy" or "glad", and also pleased about something. "Jeg er glad" means "I am happy". Add "for" (for) to say what you are happy about: "Jeg er glad for dig" means "I am fond of you" (literally "glad for you").

sentence.da: Drengen smiler og ler, han er så **glad**.
sentence.en: The boy smiles and laughs, he is so happy.

forms.en: I am happy with you / I am fond of you.

forms.da: Hun er glad for sin bil.
forms.en: She is happy with her car.

glad for.explanation: "Glad for" means "fond of" or "happy with" something or someone. It is milder than "elske" (to love): "Jeg er glad for dig" (I am fond of you) is a warm way to say you care about someone.

sentence.da: Jeg er meget **glad for** min nye lejlighed, den er stor og lys.
sentence.en: I am very happy with my new apartment, it is big and bright.

forms.en: Merry Christmas and happy New Year.

glædelig jul.explanation: "Glædelig jul" means "merry Christmas". "Glædelig" means "merry" and "jul" means "Christmas". A reply is "i lige måde" (same to you), and you can add "og godt nytår" (and happy New Year).

sentence.da: Vi har gaver og et juletræ. **Glædelig jul**!
sentence.en: We have presents and a Christmas tree. Merry Christmas!

god.explanation: "God" means "good", and it is in greetings like "god morgen" (good morning) and "godt nytår" (happy New Year). For "better" and "best" Danish uses different words: "bedre" and "bedst". To say something goes well, use "godt": "Det går godt" (It is going well).

sentence.da: Han er en **god** ven, han hjælper mig altid.
sentence.en: He is a good friend, he always helps me.

god appetit.explanation: "God appetit" means "enjoy your meal", like "bon appétit", and is said just before eating. Danes also say "velbekomme" (enjoy / you're welcome), often when the food is served or after the meal. A reply is "i lige måde" (same to you) or "tak" (thanks).

sentence.da: Maden er klar. **God appetit**!
sentence.en: The food is ready. Enjoy your meal!

forms.en: Get well soon with your cold.

forms.da: Tak, det er pænt af dig.

god bedring.explanation: "God bedring" means "get well soon" and is said to someone who is ill or hurt. "Bedring" means "improvement". You can add "med" (with) and the problem: "god bedring med benet" (get well soon with your leg).

sentence.da: Du er syg? **God bedring**!
sentence.en: You are sick? Get well soon!

god fornøjelse.explanation: "God fornøjelse" means "enjoy", a wish that someone will have a good time at what they are about to do, such as a film, a concert or a party. It is not usually used for food: for meals Danes say "velbekomme" or "god appetit" (both: enjoy your meal).

sentence.da: Vi skal i teatret. **God fornøjelse**!
sentence.en: We are going to the theatre. Enjoy!

god påske.explanation: "God påske" means "happy Easter" and is said before and during the Easter holiday. A reply is "i lige måde" (same to you).

sentence.da: Vi ses efter ferien. **God påske**!
sentence.en: See you after the holiday. Happy Easter!

forms.da: Jeg er god til at lave mad.
Han er ikke god til sport.
forms.en: He is not good at sports.

god til.explanation: "God til" means "good at" something. After "til" (to) you can put a thing ("god til matematik", good at maths) or an action with "at" ("god til at synge", good at singing).

sentence.da: Han vinder altid, han er **god til** at spille fodbold.
sentence.en: He always wins, he is good at playing football.

forms.en: Have a good trip to Copenhagen.

god tur.explanation: "God tur" means "have a good trip" and is said to anyone setting off, whether by car, train, bike or plane. "Tur" means "trip" or "ride". You can add the place: "god tur til Aarhus" (have a good trip to Aarhus). A reply is "tak" (thanks).

sentence.da: Vi tager af sted nu. — **God tur**!
sentence.en: We are leaving now. — Have a good trip!

forms.en: Have a good weekend, all of you.

god weekend.explanation: "God weekend" means "have a good weekend". It is said when parting before the weekend. A reply is "i lige måde" (same to you). On Monday people ask "Havde du en god weekend?" (Did you have a good weekend?).

sentence.da: Vi ses på mandag. **God weekend**!
sentence.en: See you on Monday. Have a good weekend!

godaften.explanation: "Godaften" means "good evening". You say it when you meet someone in the evening. It is not used when you part for bed: then you say "godnat" (good night).

sentence.da: Det er aften. **Godaften**, hvordan har du det?
sentence.en: It is evening. Good evening, how are you?

goddag.explanation: "Goddag" means "good day", a polite, slightly formal way to say hello at any time of day. Friends usually say "hej" (hi) instead. You answer "goddag" with "goddag" back.

sentence.da: **Goddag**, jeg hedder Peter.
sentence.en: Hello, my name is Peter.

godmorgen.explanation: "Godmorgen" means "good morning". You can say it to anyone, at home, at work and in shops, until late morning. For later in the day you switch to "goddag" (good day).

sentence.da: **Godmorgen**! Har du sovet godt?
sentence.en: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

godnat.explanation: "Godnat" means "good night" and is said when you or someone else is going to bed, or when you part late in the evening. It is not a greeting for meeting someone: for that use "godaften" (good evening). You can add "sov godt" (sleep well).

sentence.da: **Godnat**, sov godt!
sentence.en: Good night, sleep well!

forms.en: Happy New Year to you all.
Happy New Year, same to you.

godt nytår.explanation: "Godt nytår" means "happy New Year". Note the spelling: "godt nytår", not "god nytår". "Nytår" means "New Year" and "godt" means "good". A reply is "i lige måde" (same to you).

sentence.da: Det er midnat. **Godt nytår**!
sentence.en: It is midnight. Happy New Year!

golf.explanation: "Golf" means "golf", the sport. You say "at spille golf" (to play golf) with no "a" or "the" in front, just like "at spille tennis" (to play tennis).

sentence.da: Jeg spiller **golf** på en stor, grøn golfbane.
sentence.en: I play golf on a big green golf course.

grader.explanation: "Grader" means "degrees", and it is used for temperature: "Det er fem grader" means "It is five degrees". For below zero Danes say "minus": "Det er minus to grader" (It is minus two degrees).

sentence.da: Tag en jakke på, der er kun fem **grader** udenfor.
sentence.en: Put a jacket on, it is only five degrees outside.

gratis.explanation: "Gratis" means "free", as in costing no money: "Kaffen er gratis" (The coffee is free). Do not mix it up with "fri", which means free time or freedom: "Jeg har fri i dag" (I have the day off today).

sentence.da: Du skal ikke betale, det er **gratis**.
sentence.en: You do not have to pay, it is free.

grim.explanation: "Grim" means "ugly", for people, buildings or things. It can also mean unpleasant: "grimt vejr" (nasty weather) and "et grimt ord" (a nasty word). Calling a person "grim" is quite blunt.

sentence.da: Bygningen er **grim**, jeg synes ikke, den er smuk.
sentence.en: The building is ugly, I do not think it is beautiful.

grå.explanation: "Grå" means "gray". It is also used for weather: "en grå dag" (a gray day) is a dull, cloudy day.

sentence.da: Skyerne er **grå**, og det regner snart.
sentence.en: The clouds are gray, and it will rain soon.

gråvejr.explanation: "Gråvejr" means "gray weather", dull, overcast weather with a gray sky, but not necessarily rain. It is made from "grå" (gray) and "vejr" (weather).

sentence.da: Det er **gråvejr** i dag, men det regner ikke.
sentence.en: It is gray weather today, but it is not raining.

grækenland.explanation: "Grækenland" means "Greece". It is built from "græker" (a Greek person) and "land" (country).

sentence.da: Athen er en by i **Grækenland**.
sentence.en: Athens is a city in Greece.

græs.explanation: "Græs" means "grass". To mow the lawn Danes say "at slå græs" (literally "to hit grass").

sentence.da: Koen æder **græs** på marken.
sentence.en: The cow eats grass in the field.

græsk.explanation: "Græsk" means "Greek", for things from Greece and for the language. It has no capital letter in Danish.

sentence.da: Hun er fra Grækenland og taler **græsk**.
sentence.en: She is from Greece and speaks Greek.

grød.explanation: "En grød" means "a porridge", a thick, warm dish of oats, rice or other grain cooked in milk or water. It is normally not counted, so you do not say "two porridges". Types are named by adding the grain: "havregrød" (oat porridge) and "risengrød" (rice porridge).

sentence.da: Jeg spiser varm **grød** med mælk til morgenmad.
sentence.en: I eat warm porridge with milk for breakfast.

grøn.explanation: "Grøn" means "green". It also means eco-friendly: "grøn energi" means "green energy". Vegetables are "grøntsager", literally "green things".

sentence.da: Bilen er **grøn**, ligesom græs.
sentence.en: The car is green, just like grass.

grønland.explanation: "Grønland" means "Greenland". It is built from "grøn" (green) and "land" (country), so literally "green land".

sentence.da: **Grønland** er en stor, kold ø med meget is og sne.
sentence.en: Greenland is a big, cold island with a lot of ice and snow.

grøntsager.explanation: "Grøntsager" means "vegetables". It is used for food in general: "spis dine grøntsager" means "eat your vegetables". In shops you often see "frugt og grønt" (fruit and vegetables).

sentence.da: Jeg spiser gulerødder, broccoli og andre **grøntsager**.
sentence.en: I eat carrots, broccoli and other vegetables.

gul.explanation: "Gul" means "yellow", for example the colour of "en citron" (a lemon) or "smør" (butter).

sentence.da: Citronen er **gul**.
sentence.en: The lemon is yellow.

guld.explanation: "Guld" means "gold", the metal. It can also mean something very precious: "Du er guld værd" means "You are worth your weight in gold" (literally "You are worth gold").

sentence.da: Ringen er lavet af **guld**, ikke af sølv.
sentence.en: The ring is made of gold, not silver.

gør det selv.explanation: "Gør det selv" means "do it yourself". It is made of "gør" (do), "det" (it) and "selv" (yourself).

sentence.da: Jeg hjælper dig ikke. **Gør det selv**!
sentence.en: I will not help you. Do it yourself!
